title: Experiment: chokidar detection with and without a concurrent `next dev`
summary: Three runs of the same measurement in one disposable workspace. control: 20/20 observed, median lag 3ms, max 6ms; treatment: 20/20 observed, median lag 3ms, max 10ms with `next dev` serving on 127.0.0.1:3987; control2: 20/20 observed, median lag 3ms, max 7ms after the dev server was killed. No file was missed in any run, and `next dev` did not recompile during the content writes.

facts.network: loopback only for the dev server; npm install reached the public registry
facts.install: local to the temporary directory; no global install, no repository change

omissions.reason: The dev server ran for well under a minute. Handle count, memory growth and watcher stability over hours were not measured, and that is the actual concern behind QST-0017 rather than the burst behaviour this did measure.
The watched directory sat inside the Next.js project root. An application watching a content root OUTSIDE the app root is a different arrangement and was not exercised.
One host was available. #73 already records that file-watching behaviour differs by platform, so this result is scoped to Windows and cannot be generalised from here.

Execution was on the host with no containment, so whatever else the machine was doing during the runs is unknown. The two controls bound this rather than remove it: an unrelated disturbance would have had to affect the treatment alone.

notes: ⚠️ HOST EXECUTION, stated rather than implied. The tier-1 controller could not run this at all: the job declares `requires: { network: true }` for `npm install` and the approved ceiling refuses it before provisioning (#77), and — separately and more fundamentally — the job model has no form for a long-lived service alongside commands, so the probe is not expressible under it regardless of the ceiling. See the capability gap recorded as its own question. ⚠️ Controls before AND after the treatment, so 'no interference' is a comparison rather than an assertion: a second control isolates interference from any second-run effect. ⚠️ The workspace was removed and its ABSENCE checked rather than the removal call trusted — the same discipline the controller uses, applied by hand because no controller ran. ⚠️ METHODOLOGY HISTORY — AN INVALIDATED FIRST RUN, EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED FROM THE FINDING ABOVE. An earlier execution of this probe reported treatment 0/20 with the controls at 20/20, which read as total interference from `next dev`. It was a FIXTURE DEFECT, not an observation: both runs wrote the same filenames into the same directory, so the control created the files and the treatment only modified them, while the watcher listened for `add`. A second defect in the same version measured latency as elapsed-time-since-watcher-start, which reports the write schedule (20 files x 120ms) rather than detection lag and would have read as ~2.4s of latency on a completely idle watcher. ⚠️ NONE OF THAT RUN'S NUMBERS CONTRIBUTE ANYTHING HERE. They are void rather than weak, and the summary, outcome and omissions above describe only the corrected execution: a fresh directory per run, per-file observed-minus-written latency, and a control taken after the treatment as well as before. Both defects were in the fixture; neither touched the code under observation. ⚠️ It is preserved because the correction is WHY this result can be trusted rather than a detail about how it was obtained. The control is what exposed it — a result that dramatic, from a change that small, is a bug before it is a finding — and a probe whose only reported run is the one that worked has not demonstrated that it could have failed.
